title: Moore's law and Dennard scaling
text:
CHAPTER 6. INTEGRATED CIRCUITS AND MICROPROCESSORS
SECTION 6.2. MOORE'S LAW AND DENNARD SCALING

For roughly half a century the number of transistors on a chip doubled about every two years, while each transistor got faster, cheaper and more energy-efficient. This exponential progress is summarized by two "laws," neither of them a law of physics: Moore's law, an observation about economics and manufacturing, and Dennard scaling, a recipe for shrinking MOSFETs that explained why smaller transistors were also better. Understanding both, and why Dennard scaling ended around the mid-2000s, explains a great deal about modern computing, including why AI moved to massively parallel GPUs and specialized accelerators.

1. Moore's 1965 observation

In 1965 Gordon Moore (1929-2023), then director of research and development at Fairchild Semiconductor, was asked to contribute to the thirty-fifth anniversary issue of Electronics magazine. His article, "Cramming more components onto integrated circuits," noted that the number of components on the most cost-effective integrated circuits had roughly doubled every year since the first planar ICs, and he projected that this would continue for at least another decade. He speculated that by 1975 a single chip might contain as many as 65,000 components.

Moore's reasoning was economic. For a given technology, the cost per component on a chip has a minimum: with too few components, packaging and fixed costs dominate; with too many, yield falls (Section 6.1, Y = exp(-D A)). As manufacturing improves, the minimum-cost point moves to more components per chip. His prediction was about where that optimum would move.

In 1975, at the IEEE International Electron Devices Meeting, Moore revised the rate to a doubling about every two years. That two-year doubling, a compound annual growth rate of about 41 percent, is what people usually mean by "Moore's law." (The often-quoted "18 months" figure comes from a separate prediction by Intel executive David House about computer performance; Moore said he never claimed transistor counts would double every 18 months.) The name "Moore's law" was popularized in the 1970s, often credited to Caltech professor Carver Mead.

How big is the effect? Doubling every two years for 50 years is 25 doublings:

    2^25 = about 33.5 million

Microprocessors went from 2,300 transistors in the Intel 4004 (1971, Section 6.3) to tens of billions in the largest chips of the 2020s, roughly consistent with this rate.

Moore's law became a self-fulfilling prophecy. The industry organized its planning around it: equipment makers, chip designers and fabrication plants coordinated through industry roadmaps (for decades the International Technology Roadmap for Semiconductors) to deliver a new process "node" about every two to three years, each with transistors scaled by a factor of about 0.7 in linear dimension, which halves the area per transistor (0.7^2 = 0.49).

2. Dennard scaling (1974)

Why should smaller transistors also be faster and use less power? In October 1974, Robert Dennard and colleagues at IBM published "Design of ion-implanted MOSFET's with very small physical dimensions" in the IEEE Journal of Solid-State Circuits. (Dennard had also invented the one-transistor DRAM cell, patented in 1968, the memory cell still used in every DRAM chip.) The paper laid out rules for shrinking a MOSFET by a factor k (k > 1) while keeping its internal electric fields constant, so-called constant-field scaling.

Scale every dimension and the voltage by 1/k, and the doping up by k:

    Quantity                         Scaling factor
    --------                         --------------
    Channel length L, width W        1/k
    Oxide thickness tox              1/k
    Supply voltage V                 1/k
    Doping concentration             k
    Electric field                   1 (unchanged)
    Current per transistor I         1/k
    Gate capacitance C               1/k
    Gate delay (C V / I)             1/k
    Power per transistor (V I)       1/k^2
    Area per transistor              1/k^2
    Power density (power / area)     1 (unchanged)

Read the last lines carefully. Each transistor is k times faster and uses k^2 less power, while you fit k^2 more of them in the same area, so the power per square millimeter stays the same. Shrinking gave you more transistors, each faster, at the same chip power. That was the "free lunch" of computing: from the 1970s to the early 2000s, simply moving to the next process node made every program run faster without any change in software.

Derivation of delay, briefly. A gate's delay is roughly the time to charge its load capacitance C through the transistor's current I to voltage V: t is about C * V / I. With C, V and I all scaling as 1/k, t scales as (1/k)(1/k)/(1/k) = 1/k.

Derivation of dynamic power. From Section 5.3, P = a C V^2 f. With C scaling as 1/k, V as 1/k, and f (which can rise as delay falls) as k:

    P per transistor scales as (1/k)(1/k^2)(k) = 1/k^2

3. Clock speeds: the visible effect

In practice, manufacturers did not follow Dennard's rules exactly. They often kept voltages higher than the rules required (5 V was a standard logic supply for years, for compatibility with TTL), and they used the extra speed and transistors aggressively. Microprocessor clock frequencies rose from 740 kHz for the 4004 in 1971, to tens of MHz in the late 1980s, to over 1 GHz in 2000, and to around 3 to 4 GHz in the mid-2000s.

Then clock speed stopped rising. Desktop processors in the 2020s run at roughly the same base frequencies as those of about 2005, with short "boost" bursts to around 5 to 6 GHz.

4. Why Dennard scaling ended

Around 2005-2007, constant-field scaling broke down. The main reasons:

  Threshold voltage and leakage. To turn a MOSFET off well, the gate voltage must fall well below the threshold Vt. The subthreshold current of a MOSFET falls exponentially below Vt, but no faster than about one decade per 60 mV at room temperature (the same kT/q physics as the diode equation, Section 5.1: VT * ln(10), about 60 mV per decade). If you lower the supply voltage V, you must lower Vt too to keep the transistor fast, and every 60 mV reduction in Vt multiplies off-state leakage current by about ten. Below a supply voltage of around 1 V, further reduction made leakage unacceptable. So voltage stopped scaling.

  Gate oxide tunneling. The gate oxide had become only a few atomic layers thick (around 1.2 nm), so electrons tunneled through it quantum-mechanically, causing gate leakage.

Once voltage stops scaling, the power equation turns against you. If dimensions shrink by 1/k but V stays constant:

    Power per transistor (ignoring frequency increase): C V^2 f, with C down by 1/k, V fixed
    Transistors per area: k^2
    Power density: rises roughly by k (or worse, if frequency also increases)

Chips could not be cooled fast enough. This is the "power wall." A widely cited symptom: Intel in 2004 canceled planned high-frequency successors in its Pentium 4 line and turned to multi-core designs. The industry's response was:

  - stop increasing clock frequency;
  - use the extra transistors for multiple processor cores, larger caches and specialized units instead;
  - accept "dark silicon": on a modern chip, not all transistors can be switched at full speed at the same time within the power budget, so parts of the chip are powered down when not needed.

5. Moore's law continued, differently

Even after Dennard scaling ended, transistor density kept increasing for many years, thanks to new materials and structures:

  - Strained silicon (early 2000s): stretching the silicon lattice increased carrier mobility.
  - High-k metal gate (Intel, 45 nm node, 2007): replacing silicon dioxide with hafnium-based dielectrics of higher permittivity allowed a physically thicker insulator with the same capacitance, reducing tunneling.
  - FinFETs (Intel's 22 nm node, in products from 2012): the channel is a thin vertical fin, with the gate wrapped around three sides, giving the gate much better control and reducing leakage.
  - Gate-all-around (GAA) nanosheet transistors (in production from the early-to-mid 2020s, with Samsung first at its 3 nm node in 2022 and other manufacturers following): the gate completely surrounds stacked horizontal channels.
  - Advanced packaging: stacking memory dies (high-bandwidth memory, HBM) and combining several "chiplets" in one package, increasingly important for AI accelerators.

Node names ("7 nm," "5 nm," "3 nm") no longer correspond to any physical dimension of the transistor; they are marketing labels for successive generations. Physical gate pitches in leading-edge processes are a few tens of nanometers.

The cost per transistor, which fell steadily for decades, has fallen more slowly at the most advanced nodes, because leading-edge fabs and EUV lithography are enormously expensive. Many observers say that Moore's law in its classic economic form (cheaper transistors every two years) has slowed, even though density still increases.

6. The consequences for computing and AI

  Parallelism became mandatory. Since single-thread speed improved only slowly after about 2005, performance gains had to come from doing more things at once. Software had to become parallel: multi-threaded CPU code, and especially data-parallel code on GPUs.

  Specialization. When you cannot make general-purpose transistors faster, you get more performance by designing hardware for a specific workload. AI is the leading example. Neural network training and inference consist mostly of dense matrix multiplication, which is highly parallel, regular and tolerant of low numerical precision (Section 2.3's discussion of short floating-point formats). GPUs (Chapter 15), Google's Tensor Processing Units (first deployed in 2015 and described publicly in 2016-2017), and many other AI accelerators exploit exactly this.

  Energy as the limit. With power density fixed by cooling, the useful measure became operations per joule. Lower-precision arithmetic (16-bit, 8-bit, even 4-bit) costs much less energy per operation and per byte moved. Much of the improvement in AI hardware since the mid-2010s has come from such precision reductions and from specialized matrix units, not from transistor speed.

  The data movement problem. As Section 4.4 noted, moving data between memory and processor costs more energy than computing on it. This is now the dominant constraint for large language models, motivating HBM, large on-chip SRAM, and research into near-memory and in-memory computing.

  "Scaling laws" in AI. Interestingly, the AI field later discovered its own empirical scaling laws (Section 18.3): model performance improves predictably as a power law with more compute, data and parameters. That discovery turned AI progress into a question of how much computing hardware can be built and powered, tying the future of AI directly to the future of semiconductor scaling.

7. A worked comparison

Compare two hypothetical processors one Dennard generation apart (k = 1.4, about one process node):

    Old: 100 million transistors, 1 GHz, 1.4 V, 100 W, 100 mm^2
    New (ideal Dennard, same area): 196 million transistors, 1.4 GHz, 1.0 V, about 100 W

Under ideal scaling, the new chip has twice the transistors and 40 percent higher clock at the same power. Now the post-2005 case, where voltage stays at 1.0 V:

    Next node, voltage fixed: twice the transistors, each with capacitance reduced by 1/1.4.
    At the same frequency, power rises by about 2 / 1.4 = 1.4 times, to about 140 W.
    To stay at 100 W, you must lower frequency, or power down part of the chip.

That simple arithmetic is why your laptop has many cores at about the same clock speed as one from years ago, and why AI chips are designed as vast arrays of simple, efficient arithmetic units.

8. Summary

  - Moore (1965) observed component counts per IC doubling about yearly and projected this for a decade; in 1975 he revised it to about every two years.
  - Over about 50 years this gave roughly 2^25 growth, from thousands to tens of billions of transistors per chip.
  - Dennard et al. (1974) showed that scaling dimensions and voltage by 1/k keeps power density constant while making transistors k times faster: the basis of decades of "free" speedups.
  - Dennard scaling broke down around 2005-2007 because threshold and supply voltages could not keep falling (about 60 mV per decade subthreshold slope, leakage) and gate oxides leaked by tunneling; clock speeds plateaued.
  - Density kept increasing through strained silicon, high-k metal gates (2007), FinFETs (from 2012), gate-all-around transistors (2020s) and advanced packaging.
  - The end of frequency scaling forced parallelism and specialization, the conditions under which GPUs and AI accelerators came to dominate AI computing.
